Euclid is the author of the Elements..why: The same statement as the Elements' byline, in many phrasings. It is stated as a title-and-author pair ('Elements by Euclid', 'the Elements of Euclid', about 1,700 mentions together) and as a sentence ('Euclid wrote the Elements', 'Euclid wrote his Elements', 'Euclid wrote Elements', 'Euclid wrote The Elements', about 250 mentions together; no single sentence form passes 100 on its own except the title-and-author pairs). Wikipedia's first sentence on the Elements states it whole. It is the inverse reading (author_of) of the edited fact.

notes: Stored edit (very_unlikely): the Elements is named after Euclid everywhere. Mathematics leaves out worlds and the indeterminate query (README, Shape per topic): a fact about a number, a shape or a proof rests on definitions, so the edit leaves no consistent world to split between; the record has 4 determinate derived queries. Derived queries ask what the edit forces with the definitions held fixed; a model that still gives the old answer holds the edit only as a patch. written_by has the inverse author_of, so the near query asks it in the author's direction ("Did Archimedes write the Elements?", no before, yes after); it is the topic's only inverse near query (the inverse form of the square-root record is not determinate), and the answer is stored as the attribution to Euclid everywhere. In yes/no form it is close to the edit itself; it is kept because Rule 12 needs an inverse near query and the stored fact (the work is Euclid's) has a quoted sentence. The far query is a composition and stored (Euclid of Alexandria, the author of the Elements, thousands of mentions): where the author lived and worked for most of his life, so that the tradition that Archimedes studied in Alexandria does not make Alexandria a consistent answer after the edit. The four derived queries are compositions: they reach the new author through the description "the author of the Elements" and then a fact about Archimedes (buoyancy, "Eureka!", The Sand Reckoner, the screw pump). Each asks about the description only, so no fact stored under Euclid's name answers it. The Sand Reckoner query replaced "killed by a Roman soldier": Euclid's death is not recorded, so the original answer there was unknown rather than no; Euclid clearly did not write The Sand Reckoner. written_by licenses no transitivity, chain or inheritance, so the topic gets those from other records. The near unrelated query is the Principia (the Conics were missed by 2 models in the audit). Negation is worded "Is it true that X is not Y?" (CRITERIA Rule 6: "Is it false that ...?" confused the models).
